utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone after a long period of approximately six, seven weeks. I hope that everyone has found during this time - partly holidays but partly hard work - found what he expected to find during this period of time. Good morning to you as well, General Galic, and to the assistant of the Defence team. Good morning. I am glad to see you all here. The order of this morning will be that we first hear the parties on a motion for judgement of acquittal filed by the Defence on the 2nd of September. A response has been filed by the Prosecution on the 16th of September, together with a -- together with an authorisation for an extension of a length limit. I would like to leave all issues that are not directly related to this motion for the Status Conference to be held later on, so only if it is of vital importance for the hearing of the motion that the parties can raise issues, but otherwise they should wait until we have the Status Conference later this day. May I remind the parties that the motion was confidentially filed, so that as soon as any of the parties would touch upon a subject which is confidential, that they ask for closed session. Of course, I cannot give any forecast of what I -- what the Chamber could expect the parties to -- what issues to raise. But may I ask you to keep that clearly in mind that no mistakes are made. It has been scheduled that the Defence gets not more than one hour to make all the submissions it wants and then the Prosecution another half an hour. I hope that the parties will accept that the Chamber has read carefully the motions and looked at a lot of sources indicated in the motion and in the response. Therefore, Ms. Pilipovic, may I invite the Defence to start first.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning everybody. Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to inform the Chamber that, as you have stated yourself, Your Honour, in accordance with Rule 98 bis, the Defence -- the Defence received the Prosecution's reply to its motion two days ago. And, therefore, the Defence has agreed that my distinguished colleague will be making submission on our behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but before giving you an opportunity to make any submissions, I would like to have my laptop connected. I do not see any transcript on it. Could I have a test on whether the transcript appear. Could we have another test whether the transcript appears on my -- yes, there we are. I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may ask the assistance of the technician who is just leaving [In English] I am having the same problem. I don't know what it is. [Interpretation] With your leave, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If all the technical aspects are functioning, then, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, indeed, Mr. President and Your Honours. The Defence doesn't doubt that each person here has had the opportunity, not perhaps all the time, but certainly the opportunity to read and peruse both submissions of both parties. We received, I believe it was on the 17th of September - so that was three days ago - the response of the Prosecution. I would like to thank your Chamber for giving us the opportunity to respond to the response because I believe that one of the objectives of the session today is to respond to some of the arguments that were raised by the Prosecution, with the objective of clarifying certain matters and the situation. And the only thing that I can say is that the situation is very far from being cleared today. Now, having said that - I had the opportunity to say once, I am not quite sure at which session, but I do remember it clearly - the truths that you do not say and I believe that, Mr. President and Your Honours, in this file, the silence or rather the unwillingness to see the things clearly, that will be the worst of things. And the best way that the truths that we should be speaking about truly become -- become venomous and dangerous. The first of the points that should be examined is obviously a specific notion which is that of proof. And what is certainly been clear to everyone in the proceedings is the fact that -- regarding the facts that should be the same when we are talking about several witnesses who came to testify here before the Chamber. Well, very often we had more than one version when we didn't have completely contradictory versions, in fact, unreconcilable versions. Just one example and the simplest example would be the technical aspect. In Markale, we have a fin that was completely embedded in the hard soil, and one expert said that this was perfectly possible, when we are talking about residual speed from a technical point of view. And then another expert basing himself on military experience, and re-examined by your Chamber, categorically excluded this possibility 100 per cent. Now, after many months, when we come to this conclusion that the most important fact cannot very often be clearly established, clearly defined, clearly known, than the proof -- the question of examining the proof is being stated. In other words, in such situations, whereby, to what would your Chamber give more weight: To the fundamental notion of doubt or to that which is currently what the Prosecution is forwarding, which is the insufficient element to bring your Chamber towards a feeling of sufficient, to allow your Chamber to convict. So these are the two main questions that we are asking today -- that are being asked today. Specifically, Mr. President and Your Honours, this difficulty, and I was going to say purely factual difficulty is made even greater by another fact, which is simply the breakup of testimonies because -- breakdown of testimonies apart from their overabundance, which means that, as a general rule, we would not be able to keep in mind one single testimony, and to say, This testimony proves this, therefore, we keep it in mind because we know that we also have many other testimonies that are saying other things. And one would have to do a balancing act, not only in view of the testimonies itself, but all of the totality of these elements of the truth, in relation to the entirety of the proceedings. Now, I don't know how we can do that without losing the sight of the principle point, which is the doubt which should benefit the accused. What I have just said, Mr. President and Your Honours, certainly is also valid for what we call direct proof, if there are any, as well as for indirect proof -- indirect evidence, circumstantial and direct evidence, and what has been perfectly interpreted into English because we have these two notions, these two notions of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you allow me just to make one short observation. There seems to be a great difference between the position of the Defence and the position of the Prosecution in respect of the tests to be applied under Rule 98 bis. I take it that this will be part of your argument as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In -- up to a point, yes, Mr. President. I am going to go on about the systematic character, as an example, of what the Prosecution defined as being a campaign. What I am going to say will also be valid for the cases, the sniping incidents, as well as for the shelling incidents. When we look at the Prosecution's response, particularly item 7, and when the Prosecution response to a position of the Defence which says that your own figures, as established by your expert Tabeau, show the opposite of what you are saying because the figures keep going down. Immediately after General Galic became commander and not the opposite, and therefore, one of the Prosecution's arguments, for instance, is to say, yes, perhaps. But this because there were barricades that were set up and because there were measures were undertaken so that the funerals would take place at night. Now, I have to respond to this argument and I believe that it lacks weight. Why is that? Because if truly -- if there had been a campaign of bombardment, the Defence doesn't contest that there was firing. But if there has been a bombing campaign, what would be the difference? We know that the mortars are so-called ballistic weapons. They could reach a target behind a building or behind any barricade. It is not the erection of several containers or several lorries that would seriously provoke a cessation of a campaign. The argument, the way it was given to us here by the Prosecution, is a little bit a demonstration of the fact that there was no campaign, there was no bombing campaign. And I believe, among other things, that the Prosecution could have recognised, as they did for a case in a sniping incident, the Prosecution could have kept certain testimony; some military personnel who said that in fact General Galic had given orders to prevent his troops from firing. We cannot, at the same time, prevent the troops from firing and launch a campaign; it is completely contradictory. We have here two types of situations that are perfectly antonymic. However, I almost completely agree with the Prosecution when they say that we should look at the determining proof as a whole. This taking evidence as a whole, we cannot examine it in an isolated manner. I am referring to a quote in the response, item 12, We cannot retain, in an isolated manner, one single testimony and play it off against other. There should be a weighted mechanism, and this mechanism, if it is taken to its term, cannot but come to a very simple conclusion, that is saying that materially, the effective evidence of culpability, or guilt, has not been produced. Mr. President and Your Honours, as for the problem of terror, we have to link this question to the knowledge that the witnesses had, not only their personal knowledge, but also their actual knowledge of the military situation in Sarajevo at the time. It is incontestable and I believe that this was demonstrated that in Sarajevo at the time there were many legitimate military targets in Sarajevo. I believe that we could all say that these legitimate targets could, therefore, be targeted during a military effort by one or the other side. However, it is obvious that the civilians that happen to be there, and who are incapable of knowing where such-or-such targets were, because they were secret targets, on a psychological level they would be suffering effects of shelling or bombing, as they happen in an area, because that is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where they are, that is where they live, that's where they spend their time. But this fear that they had and that they had expressed is not necessarily the result of an illegitimate act of a firing, which would have been unlawful. This is, unfortunately, a natural consequence of what was happening in Sarajevo, and we have to remind ourselves, this was a civil war in an urban setting. I believe that we cannot deny that a civil war in an urban setting would naturally produce terror, whoever happens to be there, and certainly would have very good reasons to suffer from this terror, from this fear. But one would have to prove the will, hierarchical will, of the accused to use this fear, this terror, as means -- as military means against the population. And this -- I believe, this evidence has not been put forward. And this -- why I think that because evidence can be brought directly, but what we want to prove can also be dismissed through other considerations. And these are considerations that I would like to remind you of. I did not find an answer of the Prosecution to this, and this is the fact that if General Galic had really meant to systematically shell, he would -- he had all the cards in his hands. Everybody knew in Sarajevo that the distribution arrived every fortnight, the aid, distribution of aid, everybody know knew that they arrived in lorries. And, therefore, everybody seeing the lorries arrive in such-and-such a neighbourhood, would be able to think that there is distribution of aid in that neighbourhood, in that area. And everybody would know that the telephone lines worked and that surprisingly information during wartime circulate in this manner and it continued on for a long time. Now, what the Prosecution was supposed to do, and they could have done it was to produce all the sit-reps, all the UNMO reports in order to demonstrate that each month or every fortnight, each distribution of aid was systematically bombed, shelled. No, this was not done. There was only one case, one single case which was discussed, produced, and demonstrated. But there was no other evidence where systematically one was able to hit a large number of people. When we know - with what the Prosecution tells us - that technically speaking, that is, on the level of weapons, practically, on level of infrastructure, and theoretically - that is, in terms of intent - the army could have each time attacked these events, but they didn't do it. And here, there is a weighty argument, I believe, to demonstrate that the thesis of accident has to be taken into account and would have more weight against a strategic will. Therefore, the link that we -- that is made to the terror is the following: Any shelling naturally will cause terror. However, this terror was not a weapon of war. And I will give you proof, and this is a very far-fetched proof. This is about what was called in medical terms as broken faces, or the bent men or the bent men, the soldiers of the "Chenin des Dames" or others who suffered bombing for a long time developed a syndrome that was known as a syndrome of a bent man. These were people who, following the war, were not able to walk erect because they were afraid of shelling. And this syndrome or such symptoms were never encountered in Sarajevo. And this element, seems to me, an additional one. So for the Defence, there is no deliberate attack of civilians, as far as Defence is concerned, although it is also evident that the civilians have suffered. And we have to remind ourselves, Mr. President and Your Honours, that this war was wanted by one party only, it seems. This is the party which refused the peace. Another argument is surprising for the Defence, and this is due to the absence of written evidence of documents. The Defence says that -- maintains that General Galic never, neither did any of his officers, issue unlawful orders. The response of the Prosecution to this is that: Of course he didn't do it because it is unlawful. But then -- and this is where things become interesting -- can we seriously imagine someone who,

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...measures. So, Madam Registrar, would you please prepare a redaction. Of course, you can discuss it, but then in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to move to closed session. Now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer that, if possible, not to turn into closed session, open session again. So, if you have more issues that would have to be dealt with in closed session, then perhaps we could concentrate then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. So as to arrange time, how much time do we have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say approximately a little bit more than half an hour. You started just before quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can you wake me up five minutes before the deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall move back to these issues and to others when we are in closed session. I am referring now to item 33 in the Prosecutions response and arguments in order to show the alleged responsibility of General Galic. And they base their arguments on reasoning that is technically just and fair, but fails to lead to any conclusion because of the file. And this structure, the number of acts is mentioned; the number, identity and type of troops involved; the logistics involved; the widespread occurrence of the acts; the technical temper of operations; the modus operandi of the similar illegal acts; the officers and staff involved; and the location of the superior at the time. The first thing to do, Your Honours, is to say that the Prosecution has failed to produce evidence as to the number of acts. It is not enough to say that there was shelling in town, which caused victims. You have got to go further than this. Indeed we know that there are lawful targets in town, so you have got to go further. They had to adduce evidence on more than those five incidents that we shall come back to later on. And more importantly, the thing that had to be demonstrated was that the shelling was really the intent and will expressed to hit civilian targets, whichever they may be, and that it was not the result of collateral damage or misfiring or firing errors. I was in Sarajevo only last week, this very week, indeed on Monday. And the thing that struck me most -- I was about to say that moved me most -- was this: In Stari Grad, in the Old Town of Sarajevo, I did not see one single of the old minarets, of the old stones, that would have been hit by a projectile. Not one single minaret has been erected again. Not one single copper-covered roof was hit. Not a single steeple was brought down. But I said to myself, If you were a gunner, if you were so incredibly accurate, as the Prosecution would claim, wouldn't it be a perfect target to have a Catholic steeple, if you are not a Catholic, or a minaret, of course, a Muslim minaret, if you are not a Muslim person? Wouldn't it be a nice target? And indeed the Prosecution did not content in its case, that this highly symbolic buildings would have been taken as targets. We may have an opportunity to see this in Sarajevo, but I know that some of us have been there already. And we know that the minarets are, there that they were not hit, whilst they were supposed to be the most obvious targets to anybody who would have this in mind. So that is the first thing I wanted to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just wait -- we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will now deal with this and I will take this into account in the six or seven minutes that I left to me. Another surprising thing in the Prosecution's submissions is that they say there may have been mobile mortars - this was shown through much testimony - and that there were such mortars. This was not a legitimate reason to open what is called a counter-battery fire. This is wrong. This is absolutely wrong and untrue. It shows either a will not to see the facts as they are, or the will to hide them, which is no better. Military specialists came to tell us many times that if you have such fire then the response is admissible. Whether the mortar is a mobile mortar or not, it is up to the returning fireman to try and locate the mobile target as best as possible, but it can be hit even if it is mobile. And it would be military heresy and also legal heresy, not to say so. This alone, the number of mobile mortars, as admitted by many, this alone explains why there were -- there was much firing in a civil area that may have caused civilian victims, but as a response, was a totally legitimate and lawful act. Failing to see this would be a mistake. And to say in one's stride that the Serbian Army, whenever there was firing from the area of the Kosevo Hospital, which I went to see this week; it is still a major hospital complex. If one were to claim that the firing of which we know, that it was basically always a response to the fire open from the Kosevo Hospital, aimed at directly hitting the hospital, just as a punishment, to claim such a thing could be building a sandcastle. It is to build something out of nothing. Nothing shows this, nothing demonstrates this, and this is a pure fairytale from the accusation. You can't begin to say that we have -- we can believe any kind of evidence has been adduced if you proffer this type of claims. And this is just one example to show how the entire Prosecution case has been set up. There are some arguments that will be mentioned in closed session. One of the arguments brought forward by the Prosecution has to do with the alleged knowledge that General Galic had or should have had. And the argument is this: Anyway, even if the intelligence channels had failed to function, General Galic knew about this through international media. So this is the last resort argument, invoked by the Prosecution. Since it was said by the international media General Galic should be convicted, it boils down to this. I shall not name anybody, but we know, all of us, that we had very many witnesses, and these were not biased witnesses, they were neutral witnesses, they were major witnesses, specialist ones. And they came to testify to confirm before you that the media had been manipulated. And I am not naming anybody, but even the media could be used as a weapon of war. And we -- if we have to rely on a weapon of war to convict General Galic, nobody, at least on the Defence side, would call this justice. Last but not least, I shall focus on the five shelling incidents. There are tremendous contradictions in the Prosecution response and they show how fragile the whole case is. In the Prosecution's view, the gunners were incredibly accurate in their firing, and this allegedly made it possible for them to avoid civilian targets. And if there were civilian targets and civilian victims, in the Prosecution's reasoning, this was done with an intent. And to support this, in the very same document, the Prosecution quotes somebody who precisely claims that a mortar is not a precise weapon. Therefore, mortars should not have been used in town. And the major question that is going to be raised is basically a factual one: Is it or not possible to use a mortar? In this respect I remember one question that the Trial Chamber put -- it doesn't matter to whom it put the question -- but it was to a professional, a career military man. And the question was this: If the headquarters were in the lower storeys of floors or in the basement of buildings, what would you hit them with? Well, they mentioned a major more important calibre than just a mere rifle. And this shows, and this prompts the answer or the understanding that we are talking about mortars. So five examples brought by the Prosecution to show the absolute guilt and responsibility of General Galic. And I am going to review them, starting with the first one, the one that is sometimes mentioned, as the "football incident." I told you I went to Sarajevo this week because I wanted to see I wanted to understand. I took some photographs, and I took a photograph of this incident. I have it before me. Ten years later, this photograph shows -- I will circulate them if you wish. They are in black and white. I am sorry for that. They show me where the trenches were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an objection. I think on three previous occasions during his address, Mr. Piletta-Zanin has shared with us his observations last week in Sarajevo. That is not evidence, however, I have not objected assuming that it would be taken appropriately by Your Honours. But now we go another step. And my friend purportedly holds in his hand that he said he took last week. And no doubt, even if he does not circulate them, as he said he is prepared to do, he will still refer to what he saw last week. It is now abundantly appropriate, Mr. President, in my respectful submission, that the Defence be precluded from seeking to introduce evidence in this form from the bar table, that is, what Mr. Piletta-Zanin tells us he saw last week. If need be, I can go into reasons, but perhaps that is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the motion deals with an acquittal on the basis of the evidence presented by the Prosecution until now. If you wish to open already the Defence case by presenting evidence that night, even be contradictory to what you seek in your motion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Things are very clear. Thank you very much for that, Mr. President. Regardless of what I saw myself, a witness came to tell us that there were trenches next to the parking lot. This has not been challenged. And I can tell you, they are there, they exist. Not only do they exist, but they are very close indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I maintain my objection, Mr. President. In the face of your ruling, my friend persists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, whether they do exist or not is for the Chamber to assess on the basis of the evidence presented. I take it that you are very much in favour of that evidence that would or could establish the existence of trenches. But your personal experience is not at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I do understand. Still there are trenches. And regarding this incident, it is a fact that in these trenches, there used to be soldiers. The distance between the trenches and the parking lot is such that a firing error is perfectly possible. On the other hand, if one were to admit that the firing originated from the Serbian side, what is the state of mind of soldiers -- let's assume the soldiers are under the order of General Galic, what is their state of mind when they know that the civilians were instructed not to gather in large groups and that they can hear shouting behind buildings some distance away from trenches where firing originates from, and which are lawful targets? In this hypothesis, it is perfectly possible to have an error. Not only it is a thinkable thing, but it is also an acceptable one. It is not only acceptable, further than that, when you weigh out the positions, it becomes apparent that the doubt must prevail. Second incident coined as the "waterline incident." Investigations showed that this incident on the one hand took place basically on the front line, that it was at any rate within the military area as technically defined being some 500 to 600 yards in depth, and that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there were major military objectives in the neighbourhood. There were military objectives, but in addition to that, there were a large number of troops building military objective which was a relevant one, in other words the Dobrinja tunnel. In this instant case as well, if it had wanted to show the systematic nature of such attacks, the Prosecution could have produced all the sit-reps issued by the UN forces, could have listed them for us. If it didn't choose to do so, it is not because there is lack of personnel on the Prosecution side it is not that this is not a mission that could be carried out. Alipasino Polje here too, of course, this is a very sad event, as they all were, but what is known is this: Alipasino Polje was an important centre -- weapon factory site. This is where the mortars were made, that had been recovered and the metal of which had been melted. That is where you had the operational command and control site and that is where you had a Croat unit, the Kulin Ban unit. This is the proof of military movement, the intent to destroy mobile or fixed targets. And once again, the fact that the firing was happening in an area that was very close to a place where a lot of military objectives were concentrated, is an additional factor that will have to be retained "in favorem," "in favour of the accused," and in order to maintain the notion of doubt. I have already mentioned humanitarian aid. The same considerations apply here as for the water, mutatis mutandis, but it is mainly the very low frequently of these events that matters. So the last thing that remains is Markale. Markale is the most troubling event. If you look at the figures produced by the Prosecution, we see in one glance that there is an obvious difference between the pre- and the post-Markale time. Between the time before the 5th and the 6th February of that year, and after. We have testimony going along those lines. There is no more shelling after that date. Therefore, Markale was a very productive event for the Sarajevo forces. Somebody said, who is going to benefit from the crime? This is a question that has got to be put clearly, difficult as it may be to admit the answers to it. Whatever the case may be, we have facts. The exhibits have been manipulated it has to be said. We know that. The exhibits -- not examined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been asked to inform you that you have five minutes left. And I also note that most of what you said on the shelling incidents until now appears in the motion itself as well, which we have read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, and just a last quick word with regard to Markale, the Defence never could have access to the exhibits. What I mean, the technical, mechanical exhibits, that are in the possession of the Prosecution, and therefore, given the absence of any evidence, this is the best evidence possible. Some people do not have any interest in having the Defence being able to demonstrate what it wanted to do, which is to show in a scientific way that there is no responsibility on the part of General Galic. Can we move to closed session for a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can turn into closed session, but before doing so, I noticed that the issue I drew your attention to specifically, and this is what is the test to be applied has not been dealt with. So it is not quite clear to the Chamber whether you would accept the tests as expressed by the Prosecution based upon the case law of the ICTY, or that you stick to the tests that appears several times, that it is not proven beyond a reasonable doubt, where the Prosecution has indicated that the tests should be that a reasonable court could convict. Although, at the end of the day, it also could acquit. I have no specific submissions heard on this issue, but let's first turn into closed session. If you would like to spend another minute on that, the Chamber would be grateful. We turn now into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to respond to the submissions made by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President, at least to start, might I enquire when the next break is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered if we could finish in half an hour. We might try to do it at once. But if you say, I would rather have a break, but then a relatively short break at this very moment, I couldn't deny you, at least, a few minutes of reflection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be grateful for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that ten minutes, would that be sufficient? We will restart at five minutes past 1.00. Would the parties then please be prepared to continue -- no, we have to change the tapes, et cetera. So we will have then another short break in order to prepare for the Status Conference after half an hour. Yes. --- Break taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I already indicated to the parties, that because of the long terms the interpreters are working already they start even before we started at 11.30, that the next break might take a bit longer. We will discuss this at the end of the oral argument by the Prosecution. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I propose to respond to the issues raised by the Defence, in particular, where they have gone beyond issues raised in their written submissions, and therefore, where the Prosecution's submissions are not yet available to Your Honours. Mr. President, should you and Your Honours so desire it, we, for the Prosecution, are content to respond to any specific issues that you may have, whether or not they have been covered by the Defence. The first issue raised by the Defence was as to the relevant standard of proof, if indeed it be that, which applies to this type of decision. The submissions by the Prosecution set out that standard as has been determined by the Appeals Chamber in Josic. For instance, should you require further submissions on that, then we could do that here and now. Alternatively, we could file some written submissions on it today, although I anticipate that because it is settled law, that you will not be troubled by it. The next issue that was raised by the Defence was the insufficiency of evidence to apply the proper standard to there being a systematic or widespread pattern of behaviour. In other words, to adopt the word that appears in the indictment, whether indeed it was a campaign. The Defence referred to the Prosecution's submissions in relation to the evidence of Ewa Tabeau that the rate of casualties declined, said that that declining of figures was inconsistent with there being a campaign and the explanation, which appears in the evidence and which was highlighted in the Prosecution's submissions, does not explain it, that is, the erection of sniping barricades and other steps, such as requiring that funerals be held at night. Mr. President, quite simply, it does explain why the figures decreased. It does nothing to negate the evidence that the campaign continued. The Defence further said that there was evidence that the accused had given orders to prevent his troops from firing, and that was inconsistent in their written submissions. In support of that, they refer to the evidence of Mik Magnusson, a political officer for the United Nations. That evidence appears, such as it is, at page 8.134, commencing at line 20. He was asked in cross-examination whether it was true in around September or October 1992, that General Galic was making sure that his troops did not return fire to provocations, to which Mr. Magnusson replied, I do remember him making statements to us that he was issuing such instructions. That submission by the Defence and other submissions made during the course of the morning raise the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you on this very specific issue, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Ierace. I noted down on page 6, line 24, I hope I have taken the right screen, that I had some questions about a translation. It was my recollection that Mr. Piletta-Zanin used the word "retinir ses troupes," if I did understand him well. And I had a question mark to put, "prevent his troops from firing." So there might be a translation problem there. I am not saying that there is, but I noted it for myself to check it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that, Mr. President. In any event, that submission and others raises the issue of documentation of an official nature from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The Defence has said in its written and oral submissions that the lack of any documentation of illegal orders is evidence contrary to the Prosecution's submission. It is, therefore, appropriate to reflect on the state of evidence on that topic. There is no evidence to the effect that Prosecution or the Defence and, therefore, the Trial Chamber has a complete set of the orders issued by General Galic in the indictment period. Some documents which were disclosed from the Defence through Defence tendering in the Prosecution case have made their way into evidence. As yet, we have no evidence as to whether or not those documents are authentic, let alone, evidence that a complete set an available. In any event, as a matter of common sense, one would not expect the accused to have documented unlawful orders, in particular, as the indictment period progressed. And international attention focused increasingly on what was happening to the civilians in Sarajevo. The Defence challenged the evidence with respect to terror, pointing out that lawful warfare, naturally, can give rise to terror on the part of civilians. In our written submissions, we point to evidence which clearly distinguishes the terror that the civilians felt from the sure knowledge that they were being targeted deliberately as civilians, and I rely on those written submissions. The Defence referred to lack of damage of religious buildings, minarets, as observed by Defence counsel during his holiday in Sarajevo or, at least his recent visit. That, of course, is not evidence. The accused is not charged under Article 3, Subsection D, in any event. And for that reason, that has not been a topic, the subject of evidence from the Prosecution. But let it not thought that that did not happen. I intend to stay strictly within the proper confines of the case in making these submissions. Suffice it to say, there is no evidence before the Trial Chamber as to what occurred, if anything, in relation to the targeting of religious buildings during the indictment period. The Defence have included with their written submissions an aid memoir in the form of a map which purports to identify legitimate military targets within the confrontation lines, and around each is described a circle which purports to be a radius of 300 metres. In the oral submissions, the Defence again refers to the issue of accuracy and says that this is not clear. This is the position of the Prosecution. The evidence clearly establishes a high degree of accuracy on the part of mortar and artillery crews who were subordinate to the accused. That is not surprising, given the evidence that they were able to keep their mortars and artillery in permanent positions. So they were not concerned with initial inaccuracies with a bout of firing because the mortar had to seat itself properly into the ground. Further, the crews were firing in the same area for -- with reference to the indictment period, some 23 months. What's more, in many cases, they had direct observation of the targets. Therefore, that evidence is not surprising. The Defence responds that that is not the case, that the mortar crews were not capable of accurate firing, and point to some evidence to that effect. The Prosecution counters that if the mortar crews and the artillery crews were not capable of accurate firing, then that was surely known to the accused because of the length of the indictment period, if for no other reason. And that, therefore, was a proper factor for the crews to take into account when deciding whether or not to attempt to hit a legitimate military target. Therefore the Prosecution says, in relation to the circles which appear on the aid memoir, that that does nothing to alleviate the accused responsibility. If anything, it demonstrates, if one hypothetically assumes, the Defence contention, that the crews were incapable of such a high degree of accuracy, that in many cases, those crews had no business firing rounds into the urban areas of Sarajevo perhaps knowing full well that their first shell, perhaps their second, perhaps all of them would not hit that target but would land in those other areas. So essentially, it is a response to a Defence submission. The Defence has raised a number of issues in relation to the scheduled shelling incidents. I don't intend to respond to those issues because they are covered in the written submissions, except in relation to the first incident. My learned colleague for the Defence said that there were trenches next to the parking lot. And it seems that this was something that came to his attention over the break. That is not the evidence. The evidence is, as I recollect it, as we recollect it, that there were trenches some 300 metres from where the shells landed. And that does nothing to detract from the Prosecution case. The Defence, towards the close of his submissions, said -- and perhaps it was a mistake made inadvertently in translation -- that the Defence has never had access to the exhibits in the possession of the Prosecution, and that was said in reference to Markale. That is quite incorrect. This is a reciprocal disclosure case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I listened to the French original, and I think the Defence referred to the shrapnel pieces on the photographs as -- I think that was the argument of the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it has never been suggested that the Prosecution has possession or ever had possession of those cases. Thank you. Mr. President, there are a few comments I would like to make in private session. This would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the final point I make in open session is to simply acknowledge the submission by the Defence that there is insufficient evidence as to the proximity of military targets during -- at the relevant time of some of the sniping incidents. By "acknowledge," I acknowledge that submission was made. I take the view that the Prosecution response is sufficiently covered in our written submissions. Mr. President, I think I am within the half hour. If there are any questions that you or Your Honours have, then we would be happy to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no questions to the parties. And the Chamber informs the Prosecution that it is not asking for any additional submissions in respect of the tests to be applied. It is clear that there is a difference of view between the parties. The Prosecution has relied on the case law of the Tribunal. And apart from that, to speak some Latin as well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, "ius curias novit," "the Court knows the law," so there is no specific reason to further elaborate on that. That means that this hearing on the motion filed under Rule 98 bis is concluded. The only thing we now still have to do is to find out how long we will have a break. When I indicated that it might be a short break before, I was not sufficiently aware of the fact that the interpreters had worked already longer today, even before we started. So we now have the contradicting interest of ending early at Friday and having enough time to rest and have lunch. Since the interpreters are the most interested party, I would say, would three quarters of an hour be sufficient or would it be more? Could you please inform us what the wishes are of the interpreters' booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a different team of interpreters working from this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a different team. I was not aware of that. How much time would the interpreters need for rest? I am listening to Channel 4 at this moment, so I am not aware --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 20 minutes, Mr. President, if that is all right with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, just one short request of General Galic the Defence would like to tell you about it. His family arrived today. If it is possible, considering other reasons, it is Friday, could we please finish early today. Only with your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters would need 20 minutes. We will try to finish as early as possible, especially being informed about the family having arrived. And the Chamber, therefore, accepts that the afternoon session will be on the same tape, because 20 minutes is too short to change tapes. So you will understand that if you working efficiently this afternoon, we can stay within this one tape. Otherwise, we will need another break for changing tapes and that's -- then you are all bearing the consequences yourself. We will adjourn until five minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
